# Promoted Listings and Seller Tools: Which Ones Actually Move Product

[![Tiana Porta](https://tnl-blog-media.nyc3.cdn.digitaloceanspaces.com/2026/06/lmgyTOYK_400x400--6-.jpg)](https://www.tracknlist.com/blog/author/tiana/)

#### [Tiana Porta](https://www.tracknlist.com/blog/author/tiana/)

17 Aug 2026 — 6 min read

![Promoted Listings and Seller Tools: Which Ones Actually Move Product](https://api.viktor.com/api/coworker/app-chat/files/.eJxtzUELgjAYgOH_snM0KAzyqIXDGsxiUKcx2Tf7olnMyczovyd47f7wvh_SeyQpsfiALqU03Dxo01GZSxfry44NFW7F_ZmfknYoaAMteB3AKHS6AYX-eC0zZkqBYyyqM-fjPjHLCPWLLEjfgVdopjysQW7eTljHnHaHFQ82k3wi829G_5_k-wNP3Tgf.6VDc-YaZCwrik7Mkfrmf4_znGew)

Every marketplace now sells you a way to get seen faster. Ad rates on eBay, boosted listings on Mercari, closet sharing and parties on Poshmark, promoted placement in various forms almost everywhere else. The pitch is always the same: pay a little more and your item moves. Sometimes that is true. Often you are paying a percentage on sales you were going to make anyway.

This guide walks through the seller tools worth using, the ones worth ignoring, and the simple math that tells you whether promotion is actually buying you incremental sales or just shaving your margin on organic ones.

## What Promotion Actually Does to Your Listing

Promoted placement does not change your item. It changes where your item appears in a results page and how often it shows up in secondary placements like similar item carousels and browse pages. That distinction matters because it tells you when promotion helps and when it cannot.

If your listing already ranks on page one for the terms buyers actually type, promotion mostly buys you impressions you were already getting. You pay a fee on a sale that would have landed regardless. If your listing sits on page four in a crowded category, promotion is the only realistic way to get in front of anyone in the next week, and the fee is the price of visibility you cannot earn organically fast enough.

So the first question is never "should I promote" in the abstract. It is "where does this specific listing currently sit, and is anyone seeing it." A listing with two hundred views and no offers has a pricing or presentation problem, not a visibility problem. A listing with nine views in three weeks has a visibility problem, and that is what promotion is for.

## Ad Rates: How to Set Them Without Overpaying

Most platforms suggest a rate and most sellers accept it. The suggested rate is calculated to be competitive, which is a polite way of saying it is calculated to be high enough to win. Treat it as a ceiling rather than a starting point.

A practical approach is to start at roughly half the suggested rate on a batch of listings and watch for two weeks. If impressions climb and items start selling, you have found a working rate and you can leave it. If nothing changes, step up in small increments rather than jumping to the suggestion. The gap between a working rate and the suggested rate is pure margin for you, and on a few hundred sales a year it adds up to real money.

Rate should also scale with margin, not with price. A high value pair with thin margin because you paid up at retail cannot absorb the same ad percentage as an item you bought at a fraction of resale. Sort your inventory by margin percentage and set ad rates in bands: generous on your high margin items where you can afford the visibility, minimal on the thin ones where the fee eats most of what is left.

Watch out for compounding. Ad fees stack on top of final value fees, payment processing, and shipping if you offer it free. Four percent here and thirteen percent there feels small individually and collectively can turn a twenty percent margin into single digits.

![Chart comparing ad rate spend against incremental sales for a reseller's listings](https://api.viktor.com/api/coworker/app-chat/files/.eJyrViotylSyUkrLzEktttLXL8koSk1MKdYPdQ7NLU-KcPGoCMy0DMjKdw4yzatw109PzUstSixJTYnPzE1MT43PNUt3DSnLqjCLSEuNMIlMzotyMXYy1ytPTSpQ0lEqLU4tis9MARqfapwaalaZG5CW65GbmOtt5FuS5hTqC1QCsQ-iCLudSrUAP_w36g.P8lDGvC5q-j9rS9U7rq0NQysNzU)

Track ad spend against incremental sales, not total sales, or promotion will always look profitable.

## Offers to Likers and Watchers

This is the most underused tool on most platforms and the one with the clearest return. Someone who liked or watched your item has already done the hard part. They found it, they considered it, and something stopped them. Usually that something is price, and usually the gap is smaller than you think.

Send offers on a schedule rather than reactively. Once or twice a week, sweep every listing with watchers and send a modest discount, five to ten percent, with a short expiry. The expiry matters more than the size of the discount because it converts a maybe into a decision. Large discounts sent with no time pressure mostly teach buyers to wait for a bigger one.

Do not send offers on items that just went live. Give a listing a week to find its audience at full price. Offering immediately signals that your asking price is decorative, and buyers who watch a lot of sellers notice that pattern quickly.

Track acceptance rates by discount size. Most sellers find a cliff, often somewhere around eight to twelve percent, where acceptance jumps. Below the cliff you are annoying people, above it you are giving away margin you did not need to give. Find your cliff and stay just past it.

## Relisting, Sharing, and the Freshness Tools

Several platforms reward recency. On Poshmark, sharing pushes your item back toward the top of the feed. On other marketplaces, ending and relisting resets a listing's age. Both work, and both are commonly overdone.

Sharing is worth batching into two short daily blocks rather than spreading across the day. Focus on your top thirty items by likes and your newest inventory. Sharing your entire closet item by item every day is a real time sink with a rapidly declining return, and past a certain catalog size it simply is not possible to do manually.

Relisting deserves more discipline than it usually gets. A listing that has been up for ninety days with steady views and no sales does not need a fresh start, it needs a lower price or better photos. Relisting it unchanged just resets the clock on the same problem and costs you whatever ranking history the original had. Use relisting for items where you are also changing something meaningful: new lead photo, rewritten title, adjusted price.

The kicker on that is how eBay calculates how much they receive for "promoting" the item.  Let's say you have a 5% promotion rate, and you list an item for $27.... and it sells!    So, the buyer then pays for the item but sales tax in the amount of $3 was added on...the buyer paid $30.   What number does eBay use to calculate how much $ they receive for their "promotional activites" which according to them were responsible for the item selling?  Drum roll.....they use the $30 figure so they would receive $1.50!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

Pretty much equivalent to stealing..........
